title: Tuscany — Classic Beauty
quiz.0.question: What is Tuscany's most important red grape?
quiz.0.explanation: Sangiovese is the soul of Tuscany, covering over 60% of the region's vineyards (IWS); red wine accounts for about 90% of Toscana's production.
quiz.1.question: Which grape must Brunello di Montalcino be made from?
quiz.1.explanation: Brunello di Montalcino DOCG must be made from 100% Sangiovese (locally called Brunello).
quiz.2.question: Which category are Super Tuscans usually labelled under?
quiz.2.explanation: Because they use international grapes or non-traditional blends, Super Tuscans are usually labelled Toscana IGT.
quiz.3.question: What is the emblem of Chianti Classico?
quiz.3.explanation: The official emblem of Chianti Classico is the black rooster (Gallo Nero), representing the historic heartland.
slides.0.title: 🌿 Toscana (Tuscany)
slides.0.subtitle: Home of Sangiovese, cradle of the Super Tuscans
slides.1.title: 📍 Toscana at a Glance
slides.1.content:
Central Italy's temple of wine, cradled by the Apennines, with Florence as its capital. Red wine makes up about 90% of production and Sangiovese covers over 60% of the vineyards; from approachable Chianti to legendary Brunello, 11 DOCGs and 41 DOCs form Italy's richest appellation map.

📍
Location
Central Italy, in the Apennines, capital Florence (Firenze); vineyards on hills at 250–700 m
🌾
Vineyard area
About 58,000 ha (143,000 acres), about 6% of Italy's wine production; DOC/DOCG account for 65% of output and IGT for 30% (almost all Toscana IGT)
🏆
Appellations
52 DOC/DOCGs (11 DOCG + 41 DOC), second only to Piemonte in Italy; Brunello, Chianti Classico and Vino Nobile are the big three
🍇
Key grapes
Sangiovese dominates (60%+), followed by Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon; white: Vernaccia di San Gimignano (Tuscany's only white DOCG)

slides.2.title: 🏛️ History and Cultural Standing
slides.2.content:
From the Etruscans to the Renaissance, from Baron Ricasoli's formula to the Super Tuscan revolution — 3,000 years of winemaking intertwined with the soul of Italian civilisation

8th c. BC
Etruscan civilisation: the origin of Tuscan wine culture; vines were planted widely and wine became a key Mediterranean trade good
1716
Edict of Cosimo III de' Medici: officially delimited four zones — Chianti, Pomino, Carmignano and Val d'Arno di Sopra — and set up a commission to control production, exports and fraud; one of the world's first officially delimited wine zones, about 200 years before the French AOC system
1872
Baron Ricasoli sets the Chianti formula: a Sangiovese-based blend that laid the foundation of modern Tuscan red wine
1968–1970s
Birth of the Super Tuscans: Sassicaia (1968 vintage, released 1972) and Tignanello broke the rules — first as Vino da Tavola, then from 1992 as Toscana IGT — stunning the world and rewriting Italian wine history
1385
Antinori family business founded
1716
World-first delimited zone
11
DOCGs
1968
Sassicaia's first vintage
slides.3.title: 📜 History, Society and the Modern Revival (IWS Official Material)
slides.3.content:
From the Etruscans to the Medici

Etruscans (900–300 BC) → Roman Latini (300 BC–AD 500) → medieval "encastellation" left hill towns such as San Gimignano, Monteriggioni and Montalcino; the pilgrim route Via Francigena brought prosperity to the towns along it.

From the 13th century, for about 300 years, the Republic of Siena and the Republic of Florence divided Tuscany between them and fought constantly. Florentine noble families still in business today: Ricasoli (selling wine since the 12th century), Frescobaldi (early 14th century) and Antinori (late 14th century) — among the oldest continuously operating companies in the world.

In 1737 the Medici line died out and the Grand Duchy passed to the French House of Lorraine; in 1860 Tuscany joined the Kingdom of Sardinia, Italy was unified in 1861, and Florence was the capital until 1870. In the late 19th century oidium, peronospora and phylloxera devastated the vineyards.

Coltura Promiscua and Mezzadria

Coltura promiscua = mixed-crop cultivation: vines trained up fruit trees, with cereals grown or cattle grazed between the rows — not a training system, and not share-cropping.

Mezzadria (share-cropping) operated from the 9th century until it was abolished in the 1960s; landowners lacked capital, farmers left for industrial jobs and vineyards were abandoned. Cheap land then attracted heavy investment and, together with the new DOC system, sparked the viticultural revival and the Super Tuscan revolution of the 1980s.

🎓 Key figures for the exam

Giacomo Tachis

One of the founders of the modern Italian wine renaissance; the winemaker behind Sassicaia, Tignanello and Solaia.

Giulio Gambelli

The "father of Sangiovese", behind Soldera Case Basse, Montevertine Le Pergole Torte and Poggio di Sotto.

Chianti Classico 2000 (launched 1987)

A long-term research project led by the Consorzio to select high-quality clones of Sangiovese and other varieties for replanting across the zone; many of the best clones actually came from Emilia-Romagna.
slides.4.title: 🌍 Terroir in Depth
slides.4.content:
Mediterranean × continental climate × diverse soils × 250–700 m elevation — a varied terroir that gives Tuscany a wide range of styles, from light to powerful

🪨

Galestro & Alberese: the core soils

Galestro: a metamorphic rock — crumbly, schist-like, flaky with sharp edges and very free-draining; found in central Tuscany — Rufina, Montalcino and Chianti Classico — giving elegant aromatics and minerality

Alberese: a fine-grained calcareous marl rich in lime; mainly in central and southern Chianti Classico (Castellina, Castelnuovo Berardenga) and on Montalcino's higher slopes, giving structure

Marine sands: sand, clay and calcareous deposits left by the repeated advance and retreat of an ancient sea; Montepulciano, San Gimignano and lower Montalcino, giving a softer, rounder style

☀️

Mediterranean climate and elevation

Climate: a transition zone between the continental climate of the Po plain to the north and the Mediterranean climate of central-southern Italy; milder near the sea, inland winters are cold and summers hot (above 35°C)

Summer: hot, dry and sunny, allowing Sangiovese to ripen fully

Diurnal range: 10–15°C, greater at altitude, preserving natural acidity and aromatics

Elevation: 350–500 m is the prime band; the sandy soils of coastal Bolgheri bring a supple, fruity style

🗺️ Four main soil types

→ elegant, mineral

→ structured, age-worthy
central-southern Chianti Classico

→ fruity, supple

slides.5.title: 🏔️ Topography, Rivers, Training and Winemaking Traditions (IWS Official Material)
slides.5.content:
📍
Location
42°–44°N, the largest region of central Italy, roughly triangular: the Ligurian and Tyrrhenian Seas to the west (over 600 km of coastline), the Apennines to the north-east, no natural border to the south; it borders Liguria, Emilia-Romagna, Marche, Umbria and Lazio and includes the 7 islands of the Tuscan Archipelago, among them Elba
⛰️
Topography
Mostly hills; mountains about 25% (the Northern Apennines, plus the Apuan Alps, Pratomagno and Monte Amiata); plains only 8%, mostly coastal or valley alluvium
🌊
Rivers
Many, but short and torrential. The Arno is the longest, flowing through Florence, Empoli and Pisa into the Ligurian Sea; in the south are the Ombrone and Orcia
🌡️
Climate
The Apennines block cold northern air and create a rain shadow; southern Maremma and the islands are warmest (about 15°C average), inland winters can bring snow

✂️ Common training systems

Guyot
single/double cane pruning
Archetto
a Guyot variant
canes bent into an arch
Cordon spur
permanent cordon
short spur pruning

🍷 Tuscan winemaking traditions

Governo all'uso toscano

Dried grapes set aside at harvest are added to the finished wine to trigger a second fermentation (it can also restart a stuck one), adding alcohol, body and softness; the label must state "Governo". Still permitted for Chianti DOCG but rarely used.

Wood ageing

Traditionally large, old Slavonian oak or chestnut botti; from the 1980s French barriques became popular, and today both are used.

Consulting enologists

Tuscany adopted consulting enologists early — at first mostly French, today mostly Italian.
slides.6.title: 🍇 Sangiovese — The Soul of Tuscany
slides.6.content:
"The soul of Tuscany" — Italy's most widely planted red grape, spanning the widest quality range from everyday table wine to legendary Brunello

Key characteristics

🍷 Sangiovese flavour profile

🎨 Colour: ruby, often orange-tinged at the rim (moderate colour, strong flavour)

🌹 Nose: fresh cherry, plum, violet, tea leaf, herbs, earthy minerality

👅 Palate: high acidity, medium-plus tannin, medium body — a natural food wine

⏱️ Ageing: 5–20+ years (depending on the DOCG)

With age

🏆 Mature flavours

🌹 Tertiary notes: leather, tobacco, clove, dried rose, truffle, tar

👅 Palate: tannins integrate and round out, acidity becomes more elegant, minerality grows

⏱️ Peak: Brunello Riserva can age 30+ years

🍴 Pairing: its high acidity makes it the perfect partner for Italian food
slides.7.title: 🧬 Sangiovese Clones and Local Variants
slides.7.content:
🔴 Brunello (Sangiovese Grosso)
Montalcino — largest berries, thickest skins, ripens 2–3 weeks later, highest tannin, 20–30 years of ageing potential; the basis of Brunello di Montalcino DOCG
🍷 Prugnolo Gentile
Montepulciano — between Brunello and standard Sangiovese, medium-plus supple tannins, marked plum notes; the elegant backbone of Vino Nobile
🌊 Morellino (Sangiovese Maremmano)
Scansano coast — adapted to the warm coastal climate, exuberant fruit and soft tannins, easy drinking; Morellino di Scansano DOCG
🍇 Standard Sangiovese (Chianti type)
Chianti Classico (locally Sangioveto) / Rufina / region-wide — medium body, lively acidity, fresh cherry; the most widely planted, with 100+ clones
slides.8.title: 🍇 Sangiovese Synonyms and Other Key Grapes (IWS Official Material)
slides.8.content:
Sangiovese: hard to grow, yet the defining grape

Italy's most widely planted variety, covering over 60% of Tuscany. Its parents may be Ciliegiolo × Calabrese Montenuovo (other research points to Negro Dolce), hinting at southern Italian roots. Early budding and late ripening, it is extremely site-sensitive and prefers south-facing, poor, well-drained slopes and a long, warm season. Light to medium colour, high acidity and gripping tannins, with typical notes of violet, sour cherry, tea leaf and earth.

🔤 Five synonyms × places (frequently tested)

Brunello
Montalcino
Morellino
Scansano
Prugnolo Gentile
Montepulciano
Sangioveto
Chianti Classico
Sangiovese Grosso
Toscana
⚠️ Colorino
not a synonym
a separate colouring grape
🍷 Canaiolo (Canaiolo Nero)

Tuscany's main grape until the 18th century, when Sangiovese overtook it; it declined further after phylloxera because it grafts poorly. Still Sangiovese's chief blending partner — it softens tannin and acidity and adds perfume and mouthfeel.

🥂 White grapes

Trebbiano Toscano (Ugni Blanc in France, about 6%, gives acidity), Malvasia Bianca Lunga (Malvasia del Chianti, gives body and perfume), Vernaccia di San Gimignano (from the Latin vernaculus, "local"; unrelated to other Vernaccias), and coastal Vermentino and Ansonica.

🌍 International varieties

Present since the 19th century and greatly expanded in the last 30 years: Merlot is the region's second most planted grape, followed by Cabernet Sauvignon; Cabernet Franc matters in Carmignano and Bolgheri; Syrah is the signature of Cortona. Among whites, Chardonnay leads, followed by Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Grigio.
slides.9.title: 🏆 Chianti Tiers and Sub-zones
slides.9.content:
Chianti Classico DOCG is Tuscany's most emblematic appellation. Its three-tier system — topped since 2014 by Gran Selezione — covers every quality level, and the black rooster (Gallo Nero) is the emblem of the historic heartland.

🔵 Annata (base wine)

Sangiovese 80–100%, at least 12 months of ageing. Fresh cherry, lively acidity, approachable everyday drinking, €10–18.

🟡 Riserva (aged)

At least 24 months by law (including 3 months in bottle). More depth — leather, vanilla, minerality, €18–35.

🏆 Gran Selezione (created 2014)

Chianti Classico's top tier: at least 30 months of ageing (including 3 in bottle), estate-grown grapes only; since 2021 at least 90% Sangiovese with only native varieties for the rest, and since 2023 the 11 UGA village names may appear on the label, €35–80+.

🗺️ The 7 sub-zones of Chianti DOCG

Rufina ⭐
top quality
high and cool
Colli Fiorentini
Florentine hills
elegant style
Colli Senesi
around Siena
largest sub-zone, min. 75% Sangiovese
The other 4
Aretini / Pisane
Montalbano / Montespertoli (the last added, 1997)
slides.10.title: 📜 Chianti vs Chianti Classico: History and Rules (IWS Official Material)
slides.10.content:
14th c. / 1384
First record of a wine called "Chianti"; the Lega del Chianti defines the borders of Chianti Storico
1716 / 17th–18th c.
Cosimo III delimits the zone; Chianti was then made mainly from Canaiolo
1872
Barone Bettino Ricasoli proposes two recipes: age-worthy = Sangiovese + a little Canaiolo; approachable = 70% Sangiovese + 15% Canaiolo + 15% Malvasia (governo optional). The approachable recipe became the standard; later Malvasia was often replaced by lesser Trebbiano, damaging Chianti's image
1924 / 1932
33 producers form a Consorzio (one of Italy's first); the government delimits the historic area, enlarges the Chianti zone and creates sub-zones — the historic core becomes the sub-zone "Chianti Classico"
1967 → 2006
1967 Chianti DOC → 1984 DOCG → 1987 Chianti Classico 2000 → 1996 Chianti Classico becomes its own DOCG → 2006 white grapes banned → 2014 Gran Selezione
🐓 Chianti Classico DOCG

The hills between Florence and Siena: about 10,000 ha of vines across 9 communes (Castellina, Gaiole, Radda and Greve lie entirely within it). Rivers: the Pesa and Greve flow north into the Arno, the Arbia south into the Ombrone. Mainly continental with Mediterranean influence, 200–450 m, Galestro and Alberese soils. Min. 80% Sangiovese, with Canaiolo, Colorino, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot as auxiliary grapes; max. yield 7,500 kg/ha, among the lowest in Italy. Vin Santo del Chianti Classico DOC covers the same area.

🍷 Chianti DOCG

The wider zone created in the 1930s, about twice the size of Classico, among Italy's largest appellations by volume and exports, with wide variation in quality and style. Min. 70% Sangiovese, max. 30% auxiliary grapes (Cabernet max. 15% combined), up to 10% white grapes still allowed, governo permitted. The 7 sub-zones may follow "Chianti" on the label; blends across zones are labelled simply Chianti. Vin Santo del Chianti DOC covers the same area.

⭐ Three key sub-zones

Rufina: foothills of the Northern Apennines east of Florence, 250–500 m, part of Pomino in 1716, crossed by the Sieve river; high acidity, elegant and age-worthy. Colli Senesi: the largest, southernmost and warmest, fuller-bodied, min. 75% Sangiovese. Colli Fiorentini: south and east of Florence, historically known as "Vino di Firenze".
slides.11.title: ⭐ Five Essential DOCGs
slides.11.content:
👑 Brunello di Montalcino DOCG

Grape: 100% Sangiovese (the Brunello clone, unique to Montalcino)

Ageing: min. 4 years (at least 2 in wood), released on 1 January of the 5th year after harvest; Riserva min. 5 years (released in the 6th year)

Style: the most powerful and complex, 20–30+ years of ageing potential — Italy's summit

Price: €40–200+, one of Italy's most collectible reds

🐓 Chianti Classico DOCG

Grape: Sangiovese 80–100%, Gallo Nero (black rooster) seal

Tiers: Annata / Riserva (24 months) / Gran Selezione (30 months, created 2014); min. 80% Sangiovese, white grapes banned since 2006

Style: lively acidity, fresh cherry, minerality — Italy's most approachable fine red

Price: €12–80+, outstanding value

🏛️ Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG

Grape: Sangiovese (Prugnolo Gentile) 70% or more

Ageing: min. 24 months (at least 12 in wood); Riserva min. 36 months

Style: between Chianti and Brunello, elegant plum, excellent value

Price: €15–40, the hidden gem of Tuscany's big three

🍷 Two more key DOCGs + nearby DOCs

min. 85% Sangiovese (Morellino)
supple coastal style, €10–20

fresh and mineral, €12–22

slides.12.title: 👑 Montalcino and Montepulciano in Depth (IWS Official Material)
slides.12.content:
The birth of Brunello: the Biondi-Santi family

From the 16th century Montalcino was famous for the sweet white Moscadello. "Brunello" appeared as a local name for Sangiovese in the late 18th–early 19th century. Clemente Santi, a pharmacy graduate of the University of Pisa, pioneered single-variety planting at Tenuta Greppo, with longer fermentation and maceration, no white grapes and no governo; in 1869 his "Vino Rosso Scelto Brunello 1865" won a silver medal at the Montepulciano agricultural fair — the first official appearance of "Brunello" on a label.

In 1885 his grandson Ferruccio Biondi took over, merging the surnames into Biondi-Santi and introducing destemming, massal selection and long ageing in Slavonian oak; in the 1960s Tancredi Biondi-Santi made Brunello one of Italy's most prestigious wines. It became one of the first DOCs in 1966 (its rules modelled on Tancredi's practices) and one of Italy's first DOCGs in 1980.

🗺️ Montalcino terroir

The zone matches the commune boundary: roughly a 15 km square ringed by the Asso, Orcia and Ombrone rivers, with irregular hills and ridges converging from four sides on the town of Montalcino at the centre, 120–600 m. Sea breezes plus continental influence from the Apennines give a wide diurnal range; warmer than Chianti Classico, so Sangiovese ripens reliably. Higher soils are old, shallow and stony (Galestro, Alberese); lower ones younger and deeper, with marine clay and sand.

📋 Montalcino appellations

Brunello DOCG: 100% Sangiovese, min. 4 years (2 in wood), Riserva min. 5 years; traditionalists use large botti, modernists barriques. Rosso di Montalcino DOC: same zone, also 100% Sangiovese; Brunello can be declassified to Rosso — the prototype of the second-wine category. Sant'Antimo DOC: lets Montalcino producers make wines that are not 100% Sangiovese.

🏛️ Montepulciano and Vino Nobile

An ancient Etruscan town whose "noble wine" was drunk by nobles, artists and popes since Roman times; it declined in the 19th–20th centuries and Adamo Fanetti led a revival in the 1930s. Vineyards lie on two broad hills, Montepulciano and Valiano, separated by the Val di Chiana, 250–600 m, further inland and more continental, moderated by Lake Trasimeno; sandy soils of marine origin, more uniform. Min. 70% Prugnolo Gentile (most use 80–100%), often with Canaiolo, Colorino, Mammolo or Merlot; 24 months (12 in wood), Riserva 36 months. Its second wine is Rosso di Montepulciano DOC (no mandatory wood ageing).
slides.13.title: 🏰 Carmignano, Vernaccia and Cortona (IWS Official Material)
slides.13.content:
🍷 Carmignano DOCG — an ancient Cabernet tradition

History: documented as far back as AD 804 and delimited by Cosimo III in 1716; legend says Caterina de' Medici ordered Cabernet to be planted, and it was grown here by the 16th century. After a decline in the 19th–20th centuries it was absorbed into the Chianti Montalbano sub-zone in the 1930s; Count Ugo Contini Bonacossi of Tenuta di Capezzana led its revival — DOC in 1975, DOCG in 1990.

Rules: min. 50% Sangiovese + 10–20% Cabernet Franc/Sauvignon (in practice usually 70–90% Sangiovese); Riserva min. 3 years (at least 1 in wood).

Four wines from the same area: Carmignano DOCG, Barco Reale di Carmignano DOC (the second wine, same blend, no mandatory ageing), the rosé Vin Ruspo (saignée method) and Vin Santo di Carmignano DOC.

🥂 Vernaccia di San Gimignano DOCG

History: prized since the 13th century; Italy's first DOC in 1966 and Tuscany's only white DOCG since 1993. Towered San Gimignano, "the Manhattan of Italy", is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

Terroir: west of Chianti Classico, overlapping Chianti Colli Senesi; yellow sands, yellow clays and calcareous marls of marine origin.

Winemaking: min. 85% Vernaccia; traditionally skin contact, large casks and a slightly oxidative style, today mostly temperature-controlled stainless steel; Riserva min. 11 months, often barrel-fermented and aged.

🌿 Cortona DOC — Tuscany's Syrah

An ancient Etruscan town in the province of Arezzo, north-west of Lake Trasimeno; DOC since 1999, mostly red wines, with a growing reputation for Syrah, plus Merlot and Sangiovese.

slides.15.title: 🌊 The Coast: Maremma, Bolgheri and Elba (IWS Official Material)
slides.15.content:
Maremma is the historic coastal area between Tuscany and Lazio — once malarial marshland and a place of exile, drained and farmed in the first half of the 20th century; one of the few parts of Tuscany with large plains.

🏖️ Bolgheri DOC (northern Maremma)

A narrow strip between the sea and hills running parallel to the coast; most vineyards lie on the flat land at the foot of the hills. Sea breezes make it milder than inland. Varied soils: alluvial pebbles and gravel, marine sand/limestone/clay deposits and some volcanic material. The 1983 DOC originally covered only white and rosé; reds were added only in 1994. Rosso: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Merlot in any proportion, Sangiovese and Syrah max. 50% each; Rosso Superiore min. 2 years (1 in wood); Bianco mainly Vermentino and Sauvignon Blanc; Rosato traditionally Sangiovese-based. Before Sassicaia the area had almost no wine reputation.

⚔️ Bolgheri Sassicaia DOC

In the 1940s Marchese Mario Incisa della Rocchetta moved from Piemonte to Tenuta San Guido and planted Cabernet for his own consumption; his relative Antinori persuaded him to go commercial and brought in Giacomo Tachis. The 1968 vintage was released in 1972 as VdT → sub-zone of Bolgheri in 1994 → independent DOC in 2013. Min. 80% Cabernet Sauvignon (in practice 85% CS + 15% CF), at least 24 months (18 in small oak barrels). The name comes from "sassi", the stony, gravelly soil; it is Italy's only single-estate, single-wine DOC.

🍇 Val di Cornia Rosso DOCG & Suvereto DOCG

Hills south-east of Bolgheri facing Elba, with a climate similar to Bolgheri; focus on Cabernet, Merlot and Sangiovese. Formerly part of Val di Cornia DOC, elevated to DOCG in 2011; investment poured in after Bolgheri land prices soared in the mid-1990s.

🌞 Southern Maremma (south of Grosseto)

Morellino di Scansano DOCG: warm Mediterranean climate, min. 85% Morellino, Riserva min. 2 years (1 in wood). Montecucco Sangiovese DOCG: south of Montalcino, split from Montecucco DOC in 2011, min. 90% Sangiovese and at least 1 year in wood. Maremma Toscana DOC: a former IGT turned umbrella DOC covering all of southern Maremma, with many grapes and styles.

🏝️ Elba

Italy's third-largest island, about 10 km offshore; the Etruscans came for its iron ore, and Pliny the Elder called it "Insula Vini Ferax" (island rich in wine). Napoleon was exiled here in 1814–1815. Poor, diverse soils of granite, porphyry, limestone and schist, with terraces held up by dry-stone walls. Two appellations: Elba Aleatico Passito DOCG (100% Aleatico sweet red) and Elba DOC.
slides.16.title: 🌟 The Super Tuscans — A Revolution Against the Rules
slides.16.content:
"Rule-breaking" wines that stunned the world — from 1968, pioneering estates used international grapes to challenge the old rules, selling at the highest prices under the lowest category

In the 1960s DOC rules required Chianti to include white grapes (Malvasia/Trebbiano) and banned Cabernet Sauvignon. Pioneers who broke these limits could only label their wines as the lowest category, Vino da Tavola — yet they conquered world markets with top quality.

⚔️ Sassicaia — the first Super Tuscan

First vintage 1968. 85% Cabernet Sauvignon + 15% Cabernet Franc. Bolgheri; in 2013 it became Italy's only single-estate DOC (Bolgheri Sassicaia DOC). Bordeaux style, €150–250.

🌹 Tignanello — the perfect fusion

Created by Antinori in 1971. Sangiovese + Cabernet Sauvignon + Cabernet Franc, the first Sangiovese blend aged in small barrels. Tradition × internationalism, €50–70.

🌊 Ornellaia — an international peak

Owned by Frescobaldi, in Bolgheri. A Cabernet Sauvignon-led Bordeaux blend that stands with Sassicaia and Masseto at Tuscany's summit, €150–300+.
slides.17.title: 🚀 The Super Tuscans in Depth
slides.17.content:
⚔️ Why the rebellion began

1960s restrictions: DOC rules required Chianti to include white grapes (Malvasia / Trebbiano)

Banned: non-traditional international grapes such as Cabernet Sauvignon

The dilemma: high-quality, innovative wines were forced into the lowest category, VdT table wine

The irony: the "lowest category" fetched Italy's highest prices

📜 Liberation by IGT (1992)

1992: the Goria Law introduced IGT (Indicazione Geografica Tipica), above VdT in status and more flexible than DOC

1994: the Bolgheri DOC was amended to include reds, bringing most Bolgheri Super Tuscans into the DOC

Toscana IGT: the Super Tuscans finally had a fitting legal identity

2013: Bolgheri Sassicaia became Italy's only single-estate DOC

Today: "Super Tuscan" is synonymous with Italy's most expensive wines

Three styles of Super Tuscan

🇫🇷 International varieties

Sassicaia / Ornellaia / Masseto (100% Merlot)

Cabernet/Merlot-led, Bolgheri coast, Bordeaux style

🌹 Sangiovese blends

Tignanello / Sammarco / Solaia

Sangiovese + Cabernet, native × international

🍷 Pure Sangiovese

Percarlo / Flaccianello della Pieve

100% Sangiovese, crafted beyond the DOC framework

📘 IWS note: the real epicentre of the Super Tuscans was Chianti Classico

Two different motives

Sassicaia grew from an intuition to make a fine Bordeaux-style wine in little-known Bolgheri; the Chianti Classico Super Tuscans (Antinori's Tignanello, San Felice's Vigorello and others) grew from frustration with the outdated Chianti rules (mandatory white grapes, no 100% Sangiovese) and Chianti's poor reputation in the 1970s.

Winemaking innovations

Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc were introduced, later Merlot, Syrah and Petit Verdot; new small French oak barrels replaced old large Slavonian oak or chestnut casks; eye-catching labels and proprietary names completed the look.

Lasting impact

They forced a complete overhaul of the Chianti rules and sparked a quality revolution across Italy; Toscana IGT is now one of Italy's largest IGTs by volume and value. Many producers later returned to native grapes and a more traditional, less interventionist approach.

slides.18.description: Click the timeline and the five flagship wines to explore the legal changes from 1968 to 2013 and where each wine sits on the style spectrum.
slides.18.timeline.0.title: Sassicaia's first vintage
slides.18.timeline.0.desc: Marchese Incisa della Rocchetta planted Cabernet Sauvignon on the Bolgheri coast, opening the Super Tuscan era.
slides.18.timeline.1.title: Tignanello is born
slides.18.timeline.1.desc: The Antinori family added Cabernet to Sangiovese and aged it in barriques for the first time, breaking the Chianti rules.
slides.18.timeline.2.title: Solaia arrives
slides.18.timeline.2.desc: Cabernet-led (75%) with Sangiovese in support — an even bolder international approach.
slides.18.timeline.3.title: Ornellaia / Masseto
slides.18.timeline.3.desc: Lodovico Antinori launched a Bordeaux-style flagship in Bolgheri; Masseto, 100% Merlot, became "Italy's Pétrus".
slides.18.timeline.4.title: Goria Law → IGT category
slides.18.timeline.4.desc: Agriculture minister Giovanni Goria's reform created the IGT (Indicazione Geografica Tipica) category, giving Super Tuscans legal standing.
slides.18.timeline.5.title: Bolgheri DOC admits reds
slides.18.timeline.5.desc: The Bolgheri DOC (white and rosé only when created in 1983) was amended to include Cabernet/Merlot-based reds, and Sassicaia became its sub-zone — Super Tuscans went from "rebels" to "establishment fine wine".
slides.18.timeline.6.title: Bolgheri Sassicaia DOC
slides.18.timeline.6.desc: Italy's only DOC dedicated to a single estate and a single wine: Sassicaia went from a Bolgheri sub-zone to a DOC of its own.
slides.18.wines.0.style: Elegant, Left Bank Bordeaux style, cedar and blackcurrant
slides.18.wines.0.story: Marchese Incisa brought French Cabernet to Bolgheri and found gravel soils like those of Bordeaux's Left Bank, creating Italy's first international-style fine red.
slides.18.wines.1.style: Sangiovese-led, international grapes add structure, balanced and elegant
slides.18.wines.1.story: The first Sangiovese made without white grapes and aged in barriques; it broke the Chianti DOC rules of the day and had to be downgraded to Vino da Tavola.
slides.18.wines.2.region: Toscana IGT (next to the Tignanello vineyard)
slides.18.wines.2.style: Cabernet-led, powerful structure, long ageing potential
slides.18.wines.2.story: Antinori's flagship grows next to Tignanello but reverses the formula — Cabernet first, Sangiovese in support; in 2000 it was named Wine Spectator's Wine of the Year.
slides.18.wines.3.blend: 50% Cabernet Sauvignon + 25% Merlot + 20% Cabernet Franc + 5% Petit Verdot
slides.18.wines.3.story: Founded by Lodovico Antinori (Piero's younger brother) next door to Sassicaia, using the classic Bordeaux varieties; now run by the Frescobaldi family.
slides.18.wines.4.region: Toscana IGT (7 ha of clay within Bolgheri)
slides.18.wines.4.style: Extremely concentrated, velvety texture, top-tier Merlot
slides.18.wines.4.story: A unique plot of blue-grey clay (similar to Pomerol) on the Ornellaia estate, vinified separately as a 100% Merlot flagship. In 2012 the parent estate was renamed "Ornellaia e Masseto" and the vineyard went organic; around 2014 Masseto became a separately run estate, and in 2019 its own gravity-flow winery, dug into the blue clay, was completed.
slides.18.insight: The real Super Tuscan revolution was not "adding Cabernet" but challenging rigid DOCG rules → creating the IGT category → giving birth to the Bolgheri DOC. Once the 1992 Goria Law recognised IGT, these wines went from "rebel Vino da Tavola" to fully legal — with prices that keep setting records.
slides.19.title: 🍽️ Food and Wine Pairing
slides.19.content:
Sangiovese's high acidity makes it a natural partner for Italian food. From everyday Chianti with tomato pasta to top Brunello with white truffle, Tuscan wine and cuisine are deeply intertwined.

🥩 Bistecca alla Fiorentina

Florentine T-bone steak (Chianina beef, 1.5 kg+, rare)
🍷 With: Chianti Classico Riserva / Gran Selezione
High acidity and tannin cut through the fat; minerality lifts the meat

🍝 Pappardelle al Cinghiale

Wide ribbon pasta with wild boar ragù, a Tuscan forest classic
🍷 With: Brunello di Montalcino
Powerful tannins match the rich game; their complexities resonate

🧀 Pecorino Toscano

Tuscan sheep's milk cheese (fresh or aged)
🍷 With: Vino Nobile / Vernaccia di San Gimignano
Minerality complements the cheese's savouriness; acidity cleanses the palate

🍄 White truffle dishes

Risotto al Tartufo Bianco / Tagliolini con Tartufo
🍷 With: Brunello Riserva / a top Super Tuscan
Mature, complex aromas echo the truffle's earthy mystery
slides.20.title: 🍯 Vin Santo — Tuscany's "Holy Wine" (IWS Official Material)
slides.20.content:
Tuscany's most characteristic dried-grape (passito) wine — medieval in origin, made over years with the madre, caratelli and an unheated vinsantaia

🍇 Grapes

Mainly Trebbiano Toscano (acidity) and Malvasia Bianca Lunga (body, texture and perfume). The rare pink Occhio di Pernice ("partridge eye") is mostly Sangiovese. The most likely origin of the name: the grapes were traditionally pressed and fermented during Holy Week.

☀️ Drying (appassimento)

Healthy, ripe grapes are hung from rafters or laid on straw mats or racks (graticci) in airy lofts for 2–6 months (usually until December or even March); fans may speed the process. Tuscany's climate generally does not favour noble rot.

🛢️ Caratelli and the madre

The dense, sugary must goes into small caratelli (30–200 litres, most often 50; chestnut, oak, acacia, juniper or cherry), filled only to four-fifths. In the unheated vinsantaia, fermentation stops and restarts with the seasons in a long, oxidative process. The thick lees left in the barrel, the madre ("mother"), starts the next batch and shapes the final style. Minimum ageing is usually 2–3 years; the best are aged 4–5 years or even a decade, losing a third to a half of their volume.

🍷 Styles and pairing

From secco (dry, the rarest) through abboccato and amabile to dolce; gold to deep amber, with oxidative notes of nuts, honey, hay, dried fruit, liquorice and spice. Dry versions are aperitifs; sweet ones go with blue or hard cheeses and almond cantucci — and it is a superb "meditation wine" (vino da meditazione).

📜 The four Vin Santo DOCs (frequently tested)

Vin Santo del Chianti
Vin Santo del Chianti Classico
Vin Santo di Carmignano
Vin Santo di Montepulciano

⚠️ Don't confuse it with Trentino's Vino Santo: made from Nosiola, always sweet, usually sweeter and slightly lower in alcohol.
slides.21.title: 🏰 A Tour of Famous Estates
slides.21.content:
From Antinori, founded in 1385, to the revolutionaries who rewrote wine history — Tuscany's top estates

AN
Father of the Super Tuscans
Marchesi Antinori — Est. 1385

26 generations over 630 years; created Tignanello in 1971 and opened the Super Tuscan era. Present in every key area: Chianti Classico, Montalcino, Bolgheri and more.

Across all of Tuscany's main zones × tradition and innovation × a pioneer of Italian wine's internationalisation

A 700-year family legend

Supplying popes and royalty since the Renaissance, with 11 estates across Tuscany; took control of Ornellaia in 2005.

slides.22.title: ⚖️ Brunello vs Vino Nobile: Tuscan Sisters
slides.22.description: Two Sangiovese-led Tuscan DOCGs just 30 km apart, yet completely different in style and market position: Brunello is world-famous, Vino Nobile the value choice.
slides.22.pairs.0.title: Brunello vs Vino Nobile — Tuscan sisters
slides.22.pairs.0.intro: Two Sangiovese-based Tuscan DOCGs just 30 km apart, yet completely different in style and market position: Brunello is world-famous, Vino Nobile the value choice.
slides.22.pairs.0.left.name: Brunello di Montalcino DOCG
slides.22.pairs.0.left.soil: Diverse — Galestro schistous marl, Alberese limestone, coastal clays
slides.22.pairs.0.left.climate: Warm and dry, coastal influence, sheltered by Mt. Amiata
slides.22.pairs.0.left.ageing: 50 months (incl. 24 in wood + 4 in bottle); Riserva 62 months
slides.22.pairs.0.left.style: Dense structure, ripe tannins, concentrated fruit, exceptional ageing potential
slides.22.pairs.0.left.aromas: Black cherry, leather, cigar, spice, dried fig, chocolate
slides.22.pairs.0.left.producers: Biondi-Santi, Soldera Case Basse, Salvioni, Poggio di Sotto
slides.22.pairs.0.right.name: Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG
slides.22.pairs.0.right.grape: 70%+ Sangiovese (locally Prugnolo Gentile) + optional Canaiolo, Colorino, etc.
slides.22.pairs.0.right.climate: More inland; hot summers, cold winters
slides.22.pairs.0.right.style: More approachable, generous fruit, medium to full body
slides.22.pairs.0.right.aromas: Red cherry, violet, tobacco, leather, spice
slides.22.pairs.0.keyDifference: Brunello requires pure 100% Sangiovese and a very long 50 months of ageing, making it the "ultimate expression" of Sangiovese. Vino Nobile allows blending and needs only 24 months, closer to a high-quality wine for everyday drinking. Prices differ by 3–5×, yet Vino Nobile often beats entry-level Brunello on value.
slides.23.title: 🍷 Label Example: Chianti Classico DOCG
slides.23.caption: Ruffino Riserva Ducale Chianti Classico DOCG 2008 — note the black rooster (Gallo Nero) seal on the neck and the word "Riserva", marking the historic heartland and the aged tier.
slides.24.title: 🍷 Label Example: Brunello di Montalcino DOCG
slides.24.caption: Castello Banfi Brunello di Montalcino DOCG 2008 — Tuscany's most powerful expression of Sangiovese; the label makes the 100% Sangiovese rule clear.
slides.25.title: 🍷 Label Example: the Super Tuscan Tignanello
slides.25.caption: Antinori Tignanello — the landmark Super Tuscan first made in 1971; its label says only "Toscana IGT", not DOCG, a perfect example of how Super Tuscans broke the old rules.
slides.26.title: 🎓 Key Takeaways
slides.26.points.0: ✓ Sangiovese is the soul of Tuscany (60%+ of plantings); local synonyms: Brunello, Morellino, Prugnolo Gentile, Sangioveto
slides.26.points.1: ✓ Brunello = the most powerful, Chianti Classico = the most classic
slides.26.points.2: ✓ Chianti Classico became its own DOCG in 1996, banned white grapes in 2006 and added the top Gran Selezione tier in 2014; Chianti DOCG has 7 sub-zones
slides.26.points.3: ✓ The Super Tuscans broke with tradition to create new styles; Sassicaia (1968) led the way
slides.26.points.4: ✓ In 1716 Cosimo III de' Medici delimited Chianti, Pomino, Carmignano and Val d'Arno di Sopra — among the world's first official wine zones
slides.26.points.5: ✓ Brunello di Montalcino: 100% Sangiovese, min. 4 years of ageing (released in the 5th year); Vino Nobile: min. 70% Prugnolo Gentile, 24 months
slides.26.points.6: ✓ Carmignano traditionally includes 10–20% Cabernet; Vernaccia di San Gimignano was Italy's first DOC and is Tuscany's only white DOCG
slides.26.points.7: ✓ Vin Santo is made from dried Trebbiano Toscano + Malvasia Bianca Lunga and aged oxidatively for years in caratelli with the madre; it has 4 dedicated DOCs
slides.26.points.8: ✓ Coastal Bolgheri has risen to become an ideal home for international grapes
slides.26.points.9: ✓ Historic family estates (Antinori / Frescobaldi) coexist with a spirit of innovation
slides.26.points.10: ✓ Sangiovese's high acidity makes it the king of pairings with Italian food
slides.27.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
slides.27.questions.0.question: The black rooster (Gallo Nero) emblem is the symbol of which appellation?
slides.27.questions.0.explanation: The black rooster (Gallo Nero) is the official emblem of Chianti Classico DOCG, symbolising the historic heartland between Florence and Siena.
slides.27.questions.1.question: What is the minimum ageing requirement for Brunello di Montalcino DOCG?
slides.27.questions.1.explanation: IWS: Brunello di Montalcino must age at least 4 years (at least 2 in wood) and may be released only on 1 January of the 5th year after harvest; Riserva at least 5 years (released in the 6th year) — Italy's longest minimum ageing.
slides.27.questions.2.question: Which of the following describe the Super Tuscans? (Select all that apply)
slides.27.questions.2.options.0: A. They use non-traditional grapes such as Cabernet Sauvignon or Merlot
slides.27.questions.2.options.1: B. They were first labelled Vino da Tavola, and most moved to Toscana IGT after 1992
slides.27.questions.2.options.2: C. They were born as innovative experiments in the late 1960s and 1970s
slides.27.questions.2.options.3: D. The rules require them to be 100% Sangiovese
slides.27.questions.2.explanation: Super Tuscans use international grapes or non-traditional blends. Because they did not meet the DOC rules, they were first labelled Vino da Tavola and later Toscana IGT; they emerged from innovative experiments starting in 1968.
slides.27.questions.3.question: What is Sangiovese's standing in Italian viticulture?
slides.27.questions.3.options.1: B. Italy's most widely planted red grape
slides.27.questions.3.options.2: C. A newly introduced international variety
slides.27.questions.3.options.3: D. Mainly used for white wine
slides.27.questions.3.explanation: Sangiovese is Italy's most widely planted red grape, grown not only in Tuscany but widely in Umbria, Marche, Emilia-Romagna and elsewhere.
slides.27.questions.4.question: Which of these are Tuscan red DOCGs? (Select all that apply)
slides.27.questions.4.explanation: Brunello di Montalcino, Chianti Classico and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano are all Tuscan red DOCGs. Barolo is a Piemonte DOCG.
slides.27.questions.5.question: Which of the following is NOT a synonym for Sangiovese?
slides.27.questions.5.explanation: Colorino is a separate colouring grape. Brunello (Montalcino), Morellino (Scansano), Prugnolo Gentile (Montepulciano) and Sangioveto (Chianti Classico) are all local names for Sangiovese.
slides.27.questions.6.question: Who revived Carmignano as an independent appellation in the second half of the 20th century (DOC 1975, DOCG 1990)?
slides.27.questions.6.explanation: Count Ugo Contini Bonacossi of Tenuta di Capezzana led Carmignano out of Chianti Montalbano: DOC in 1975, DOCG in 1990.
slides.27.questions.7.question: Which of the seven Chianti DOCG sub-zones was added last (1997)?
slides.27.questions.7.explanation: Montespertoli, south of Empoli, became a sub-zone only in 1997; the others were established in 1932.
slides.27.questions.8.question: Which of these DOCs are dedicated exclusively to Vin Santo? (Select all that apply)
slides.27.questions.8.options.0: A. Vin Santo del Chianti Classico
slides.27.questions.8.explanation: Tuscany's four Vin Santo DOCs are Vin Santo del Chianti, Vin Santo del Chianti Classico, Vin Santo di Carmignano and Vin Santo di Montepulciano. Montalcino's traditional sweet wine is Moscadello.
slides.27.questions.9.question: What is "coltura promiscua"?
slides.27.questions.9.options.1: B. A traditional Tuscan vine-training system
slides.27.questions.9.options.3: D. The starter culture for Vin Santo
slides.27.questions.9.explanation: Coltura promiscua is mixed-crop cultivation: vines trained up fruit trees, with cereals grown or cattle grazed between the rows. Share-cropping is mezzadria, and Vin Santo's starter is the madre.
